notes.text: Then Paul standing in the midst of the Areopagus — An ample theatre; said - Giving them a lecture of natural divinity, with admirable wisdom, acuteness, fulness, and courtesy. They inquire after new things: Paul in his divinely philosophical discourse, begins with the first, and goes on to the last things, both which were new things to them. He points out the origin and the end of all things, concerning which they had so many disputes, and equally refutes both the Epicurean and Stoic. I perceive - With what clearness and freedom does he speak! Paul against Athens!

I found an altar — Some suppose this was set up by Socrates, to express in a covert way his devotion to the only true God, while he derided the plurality of the heathen gods, for which he was condemned to death: and others, that whoever erected this altar, did it in honour to the God of Israel, of whom there was no image, and whose name Jehovah was never made known to the idolatrous Gentiles. Him proclaim I unto you - Thus he fixes the wandering attention of these blind philosophers; proclaiming to them an unknown, and yet not a new God.
God who made the world — Thus is demonstrated even to reason, the one true, good God; absolutely different from the creatures, from every part of the visible creation.

Neither is he served as though he needed any thing — or person - The Greek word equally takes in both. To all - That live and breathe;-in him we live; and breathe - In him we move. By breathing life is continued. I breathe this moment: the next is not in my power: and all things - For in him we are. So exactly do the parts of this discourse answer each other.

He hath made of one blood the whole nation of men — By this expression the apostle showed them in the most unaffected manner, that though he was a Jew, be was not enslaved to any narrow views, but looked on all mankind as his brethren: having determined the times - That it is God who gave men the earth to inhabit, Paul proves from the order of times and places, showing the highest wisdom of the Disposer, superior to all human counsels. And the bounds of their habitation - By mountains, seas, rivers, and the like.

If haply — The way is open; God is ready to be found. But he will lay no force upon man; they might feel after him - This is in the midst between seeking and finding. Feeling being the lowest and grossest of all our senses, is fitly applied to the low knowledge of God; though he be not far from every one of us - We need not go far to seek or find him. He is very near us; in us. It is only perverse reason which thinks he is afar off.

In him — Not in ourselves, we live, and move, and have our being - This denotes his necessary, intimate, and most efficacious presence. No words can better express the continual and necessary dependence of all created beings, in their existence and all their operations, on the first and almighty cause, which the truest philosophy as well as divinity teaches. As certain also of your own poets have said - Aratus, whose words these are, was an Athenian, who lived almost three hundred years before this time. They are likewise to be found, with the alteration of one letter only, in the hymn of Cleanthes to Jupiter or the supreme being, one of the purest and finest pieces of natural religion in the whole world of Pagan antiquity.

We ought not to think — A tender expression especially in the first per son plural. As if he had said, Can God himself be a less noble being than we who are his offspring? Nor does he only here deny, that these are like God, but that they have any analogy to him at all, so as to be capable of representing him.

The times of ignorance — What! does he object ignorance to the knowing Athenians? Yes, and they acknowledge it by this very altar. God overlooked - As one paraphrases, "The beams of his eye did in a manner shoot over it." He did not appear to take notice of them, by sending express messages to them as he did to the Jews. But now - This day, this hour, saith Paul, puts an end to the Divine forbearance, and brings either greater mercy or punishment. Now he commandeth all men everywhere to repent - There is a dignity and grandeur in this expression, becoming an ambassador from the King of heaven. And this universal demand of repentance declared universal guilt in the strongest manner, and admirably confronted the pride of the haughtiest Stoic of them all. At the same time it bore down the idle plea of fatality. For how could anyone repent of doing what he could not but have done?

He hath appointed a day in which he will judge the world — How fitly does he speak this, in their supreme court of justice? By the man - So he speaks, suiting himself to the capacity of his hearers. Whereof he hath given assurance to all men, in that he hath raised him from the dead - God raising Jesus demonstrated hereby, that he was to be the glorious Judge of all. We are by no means to imagine that this was all which the apostle intended to have said, but the indolence of some of his hearers and the petulancy of others cut him short.

glossa.text:
*Men of Athens,* etc. *What you worship in ignorance, that I preach.* He answers to that which they had said or had put forward: *Thou bringest in certain new things,* as if he said: The new things which I bring in you have among your old ones. And this he says for persuasion, lest they refute his words as new.

*To an unknown God. ((RAB.))* That is, to the true God, whom no one knows as he is, etc., *as far as* that which is passed over in silence, or it was simply written: *To an unknown God.*

*God, who made the world.* Note the order of this disputation, because first he teaches that one God is the author of the world, of all things, in whom we live, and are moved, and are, whose offspring also we are: so that not only for light and life, but also for the kinship of race, he may be shown to be one who ought to be loved.
*Of one all the race of men.* In the Greek: *of one blood,* because blood designates the propagation of the flesh, and by the flesh man is understood.

*For in him we live. ((AUG.))* Because he works that in us, which is that *we live, are moved, and are,* etc., *as far as* because what is not of him, of whom it is said: *Of him, and by him, and in him are all things ((Rom. II))*?

*As also certain of your own poets.* To those who did not receive the prophets he speaks the testimony, not of Moses, not of Isaias, or of any of the prophets, but of their own authors, setting down a verse of Aratus, and out of their own false things, which they could not contradict, he preserves and confirms his own truth. *For his,* etc. This testimony was taken from the poet Aratus, not from the divine page, lest he should seem to bring in new things.
*Being therefore,* etc., *we ought not. ((RAB.))* Man is in the middle, having God as higher, gold from silver, with the rest of this kind as lower, which ought not to be compared to him.
*God despising. ((ID.))* That is, pardoning them as venial, and then despising, that is, judging them unworthy of his notice.
*Giving faith to all. ((ID.))* By the example of his own resurrection: or, he has appointed to judge, and afterward it is to be joined thus, giving faith to all that they shall rise again.

notes.text: Proved us — As it were in a burning furnace; and with a design to purge out our dross.
Net — Which our enemies laid for us.
To ride — To use us like slaves.
I will go — One speaks in the name of all the rest. Incense - With the fat of rams, which is no less pleasing to God than incense.

Iniquity — Any sin. In heart - If my heart had been false to God, although I might have forborne outward acts. If I had been guilty of that, by heart was set upon sin, or I desired only that which I resolved in my heart to spend upon my lusts. A prayer for Israel, ver. 1. For the conversion of the Gentiles, ver. 2-5. A prospect of glorious times, ver. 6, 7. To the chief musician on Neginoth, A psalm or song.

glossa.text: *Bless ye.* ((CAS.)) Diapsalma. He admonishes the Gentiles to bless God, who, although he tries them by tribulations, yet leads them to the kingdom; for these things seem to stand in the way of the promised resurrection. *Make ye heard.* ((AUG.)) Openly, so that he who loves God loves his neighbour also. *The voice of his praise.* Which the Father speaks of the Son: *This is my Son.*

*Who hath set my soul. ((Ibid.))* Here he enumerates for what causes he ought to be preached.

 *For thou hast proved us.* [n: (AUG.)] Thou hast not given us over unto commotion. Because thou hast proved us, thou hast not cast us headlong, thou hast proved us by adversities, by the fire of charity, which does not suffer us to feel torments, or, thou hast tried us by the fire of tribulation, etc.
*A snare.* ((AUG.)) Not one that deceives, but one that proves. *We have passed over.* ((CAS.; AUG.)) Thou all these things, and we, etc., *as far as* this happens to us in temptations.

*I will go in.* ((CAS.)) Behold what good things against the evils that went before, that he may strengthen us. *In holocausts.* That is, that I may offer myself to thy sight, etc., *as far as* but he withdrew that which is dearer, himself.

*They have distinguished.* ((AUG.)) He distinguishes who says that he himself is nothing, and God all things; and that he himself has need of God, not God of him. *And my mouth hath spoken.* Whom before all men I have declared to prevail above all other vows in my tribulation, not overcome by tribulation.

*Marrowy holocausts.* Myself, with the marrow of inmost love. *With the burnt offering of rams. ((Ibid.))* Or, with *the burnt offering,* which is prayer; and with *rams,* because the leaders of the flock pray most of all for the flock. *With the burnt offering.* ((HIER., AUG.)) With the prayer of the Apostles, because that pleases God which is done by their tradition. Or with the burning and destruction of brutishness and of resistance. Oxen; stiffness of neck; *with he-goats,* wantonness; these vices being slain in me. *I will offer thee oxen.* ((AUG.)) If those who thresh are offered, yet they do not remain sinners: but healed through penance they are offered; and they not by themselves, but rather joined to the oxen, because they have made themselves friends of the mammon of iniquity.

*Come ye, hear.* Diapsalma. All things now being set forth, he again admonishes not so much the untaught, but the devout, that by the example of his own deliverance they may trust the more in the Lord: blessing him for the hearing of his prayer. So do I, and O ye Gentiles, *come ye.*

*To him I have cried with my mouth.* ((CAS.)) He sets forth how great things he did for his own soul, subjoining: *To him,* etc. This he did for my soul, that I should cry to him, while the Gentiles cried to idols: and what I speak without I have within, and not iniquity, because thus is the purity of prayer, it is heard. *I have cried and exalted in my heart.* ((AUG.)) That is, I have preached him publicly, and confessed him in secret. What I have in the mouth, this I have in the heart also: yet *I will offer marrowy holocausts.* By these two the Christian is made perfect.
*Mine.* That is a man's own which is not perverse; he sets it forth with reason, that they may learn to labour first before they seek the reward.
*My prayer,* etc. These two are joined together; if prayer is not suspended, neither is mercy deferred.

notes.text: Who is he that will harm you — None can.
But if ye should suffer — This is no harm to you, but a good. Fear ye not their fear - The very words of the Septuagint, Isaiah viii, 12, 13. Let not that fear be in you which the wicked feel.

But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts — Have an holy fear, and a full trust in his wise providence. The hope - Of eternal life. With meekness - For anger would hurt your cause as well as your soul. And fear - A filial fear of offending God, and a jealousy over yourselves, lest ye speak amiss.

Having a good conscience — So much the more beware of anger, to which the very consciousness of your innocence may betray you. Join with a good conscience meekness and fear, and you obtain a complete victory. Your good conversation in Christ - That is, which flows from faith in him.
It is infinitely better, if it be the will of God, ye should suffer. His permissive will appears from his providence.

For — This is undoubtedly best, whereby we are most conformed to Christ. Now Christ suffered once - To suffer no more. For sins - Not his own, but ours. The just for the unjust - The word signifies, not only them who have wronged their neighbours, but those who have transgressed any of the commands of God; as the preceding word, just, denotes a person who has fulfilled, not barely social duties, but all kind of righteousness. That he might bring us to God - Now to his gracious favour, hereafter to his blissful presence, by the same steps of suffering and of glory. Being put to death in the flesh - As man. But raised to life by the Spirit - Both by his own divine power, and by the power of the Holy Ghost.

By which Spirit he preached — Through the ministry of Noah. To the spirits in prison - The unholy men before the flood, who were then reserved by the justice of God, as in a prison, till he executed the sentence upon them all; and are now also reserved to the judgment of the great day.
When the longsuffering of God waited — For an hundred and twenty years; all the time the ark was preparing: during which Noah warned them all to flee from the wrath to come.

The antitype whereof — The thing typified by the ark, even baptism, now saveth us - That is, through the water of baptism we are saved from the sin which overwhelms the world as a flood: not, indeed, the bare outward sign, but the inward grace; a divine consciousness that both our persons and our actions are accepted through him who died and rose again for us.
Angels and authorities and powers — That is, all orders both of angels and men.

glossa.text: *And who is he. ((BEDA.))* Therefore you are bound *debitis*; read *debetis*, "you ought" to turn aside from evil and to do good, because no one can draw you back from the good, nor from the crown, if you shall have willed to persist, nay rather they profit you while they wish to harm.
*But the fear.* In the future you shall be blessed, but in the present *fear ye not their fear,* that is, those things in them which can seem to be feared, such as royal power, and the like.

*But the Lord.* The holiness of Christ; behold with the inmost affection of the heart of how incomprehensible a glory it is, and so sanctify Christ himself in you, that he depart not from the memory, not from the love. He who does not consider this holiness fails before the snares of the enemy. *To every one that asketh.* To him that is willing to receive reasonable moneys on loan, let us not refuse. Whence Paul: *Walk in wisdom for the sake of them that are without, knowing how it behoveth to answer every one.* For they that are without, that is, they that are not yet faithful, wish to know something of the hope which is in you. He therefore who presides over the ecclesiastical teaching, let him teach those that are patient, let him stop the mouths of those that resist.
*But with modesty.* In the very knowledge of doctrine he admonishes that the manner of teaching be observed, that humility may be shown both in living and in speaking.
*It is better. ((BEDA.))* So ought you to bear with your slanderers and to confound them, etc., *as far as* he is removed and is prepared for eternal vengeance.

*He might offer to God. ((ID.))* Because even then, if any had been willing to believe at the preaching of the Lord (which they set forth through the life of the faithful), he rejoiced to offer them to God the Father. But if any disparaged the good as though they were evildoers, at the imminence of the flood they were confounded.

*In prison. ((ID.))* They who have their sense darkened with shadows are rightly said to be shut up in prison even in this life, and in this inward prison of the mind they are weighed down by unjust works, until, loosed from the flesh, they are cast into the exterior darkness of eternal damnation. The just also have a prison here, but one of tribulations, whereas the reprobate have one of vices.

*When they waited for the patience of God.* When the patience of God invited them to repentance, sparing them for the hundred years in which Noe was building the ark, by which was shown what was to come to pass in the world. They therefore did not use the patience of God unto repentance, but awaited it as though it were going to endure for ever. *Noe.* Noe is interpreted rest, and signifies Christ who gives to his faithful the rest of souls.

*When the ark was a building. ((BEDA.))* As the ark was built of planed timbers, so the Church of the gathering of faithful souls: and as, when the world was perishing, few were saved by water: so, in comparison with those that perish, small is the number of the elect, because narrow is the way which leads to life, and few there are that find it.

*Whereunto you also of the like form.* Baptism makes men safe, baptism, I say, *of the like form,* that is, likened in all things to that ark, because whatsoever is there done carnally, here is done spiritually.

*Not the putting away of the flesh,* etc. I do not say that that baptism saves where there is only *a putting away of the filth of the flesh,* that is, where the flesh only is washed outwardly (which the heretics had), but where there is *the examination of a pure conscience,* that is, where a good conscience of him that is to be baptized is asked and required by the baptizer: because such a baptism saves, another kills; the examination has been made tending unto God, that through a good conscience he may be made one with God.

*Swallowing up death. ((BEDA.))* What we swallow down, we bring it about that, taken into our bodies, it nowhere appears: so the Lord utterly consumed death, that it might avail nothing against him, and, the appearance of a true body remaining, the stain of the ancient frailty was absent. Which is promised to us also, whence he adds, *that we also might be made heirs of eternal life. The angels being made subject to him.* We do not doubt that the angels were always subject to the Son of God, but he here makes mention of the subjection for this reason, that he might show the assumed humanity so exalted in the resurrection that it is preferred before every power of angelic dignity. Whence, *thou hast subjected all things under his feet ((Psal. VIII))*.

notes.text: If ye love me, keep my commandments — Immediately after faith he exhorts to love and good works.

And I will ask the Father — The 21st verse, ver. 21, shows the connection between this and the preceding verses. And he will give you another Comforter - The Greek word signifies also an advocate, instructer, or encourager. Another - For Christ himself was one. To remain with you forever - With you, and your followers in faith, to the end of the world.

The Spirit of truth — Who has, reveals, testifies, and defends the truth as it is in Jesus. Whom the world - All who do not love or fear God, cannot receive, because it seeth him not - Having no spiritual senses, no internal eye to discern him; nor consequently knoweth him. He shall be in you - As a constant guest. Your bodies and souls shall be temples of the Holy Ghost dwelling in you.

I will not leave you orphans — A word that is elegantly applied to those who have lost any dear friend. I come to you - What was certainly and speedily to be, our Lord speaks of as if it were already.

But ye see me — That is, ye shall certainly see me. Because I live, ye shall live also - Because I am the living One in my Divine nature, and shall rise again in my human nature, and live for ever in heaven: therefore ye shall live the life of faith and love on earth, and hereafter the life of glory.
At that day — When ye see me after my resurrection; but more eminently at the day of pentecost.
He that hath my commandments — Written in his heart. I will manifest myself to him - More abundantly.

glossa.text: *If you love me.* How does he admonish them to love and to keep the commandments, that they may receive the Spirit, whom unless they have they cannot love and keep? But what they had in less measure, secretly, they were to receive more abundantly, openly, so that what they had might become known to them.

*And I will ask the Father. ((THEOPH.))* I will ask, that is, I will beseech the Father, and he will send you another Paraclete, etc., *as far as* that the Paraclete Spirit and his condescending grace may wholly come upon them, he says to them: *I will ask the Father.*

*Because it seeth him not,* etc. The lovers of the world have not spiritual eyes wherewith they might see the Holy Spirit. Nor indeed can they see him with carnal eyes, because the Holy Spirit did not appear clothed in humanity. *And in you.* He shall be in you; he shall not abide in order to be, because to be somewhere is prior to abiding. Let no one therefore think that he so abides as a guest visibly with another; but in them he can be known, not by others.
*I will not leave.* The Spirit shall not be given in my stead in such a way that I too am not with you. Orphani is Greek, pupilli is Latin.

*Yet a little while, and the world.* But the world, which now sees with the eyes of the flesh, after a little while shall not see, because when raised again he did not show himself to them; but the whole time is little, and when it is ended the impious man shall be taken away, that he may not see the glory of God, which the just shall see. *Because I live, and you shall live.* He uses the present, because his resurrection is soon to be. Of those he uses the future, whose resurrection is to be at the end.
*And you in me, and I in you.* This is so now, and is known after a fashion through faith; but then it shall be known through sight, when this conjunction shall be perfected which is now begun.

*He that hath,* etc. Not only you apostles shall live and shall know, but also whosoever has [them] in memory and keeps [them] in life. Or, he has by doing, keeps by persevering. Or he who has [them] in his discourses keeps [them] in his manners. Or, he has by hearing, keeps by doing. *And I will love him.* To this end will I love him, that I may manifest [myself], because even now he loves, but not to this end, but rather that we may believe and keep the commandments, that we may deserve what we may afterwards receive. *And I will manifest to him.* He who has my commandment, he knows me, and this is [what stands] there: *I will manifest myself to him.* But he sets first the cause of the commandment, because he loves me; and he who loves me, my Father will love him, and because the Father [loves him], then I too will love him, and thence comes the manifestation.

registers.label: Spare
lines: I will not leave you orphaned, he said.
He is coming to us still.
The Father will send another Advocate,
the Spirit of truth, to be with us always.
In him we live and move and have our being.
We are never beyond his keeping.
Christ is risen!
Christ is risen, alleluia!

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Come, all you who have felt left behind, who know what an empty house can feel like; hear the promise — I will not leave you orphaned.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
He is sending another Advocate, the Spirit of truth, to live not far off but near, with you and in you.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
For in God we live and move and have our being; there is no road that runs past the edge of his love.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
So come and bless our God, you peoples; he has kept us among the living and held our feet from slipping.
Christ is risen, alleluia!

lines: I will not leave you orphaned, says the Lord.

Christ is risen, alleluia!
Bless our God, you peoples. Come, let us worship.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
